surface_summary: Reginald Templeton is found murdered on his yacht at Marsh Quay. Initial suspects include an artist who fled suddenly, a diamond dealer who left town abruptly, and a retired cigar merchant with suspicious behavior. The case involves mysterious cigar bands, a walking-stick, and missing diamonds.
accepted_facts: Templeton was murdered on his yacht late Saturday night or early Sunday morning
Templeton had diamonds and incriminating papers related to Norwood’s embezzlement
A cigar band found at the scene was changed during the inquest
The walking-stick found in the dinghy did not belong to Templeton
inferred_conclusions: The artist Grayson was the murderer due to his sudden departure and cigar evidence
Isaac Moss was guilty because he fled and had access to the yacht
Joseph Proctor was the culprit because he changed the cigar band and had opportunity
mechanism_description: Norwood arranged a secret meeting with Templeton to obtain incriminating papers. He accompanied Templeton back to the yacht, where he murdered him with a dagger. Norwood then staged the scene by leaving his walking-stick in the dinghy and changing the cigar band at the inquest to mislead investigators. He used the canoe and dinghy to create an alibi and escape unnoticed.
delivery_path: Norwood met Templeton in Frattenbury and walked back with him to Marsh Quay
They boarded the yacht together; Norwood was smoking a cigar
Norwood used a dagger to fatally stab Templeton in the cabin
Norwood searched Templeton’s pockets and took papers but missed the diamond bag
Norwood rowed back in the dinghy, leaving his walking-stick behind
He returned the dinghy to the yacht using a canoe to avoid suspicion
At the inquest, Norwood swapped the cigar band to implicate another suspect
outcome_result: Francis Norwood is arrested for the murder of Reginald Templeton and later commits suicide in custody.

false_assumption.statement: The murder was committed by someone who boarded the yacht before Templeton returned.
false_assumption.why_it_seems_reasonable: The presence of the walking-stick in the dinghy and the open cabin door suggested the killer was already aboard. Witnesses assumed the murderer was waiting on the yacht.
false_assumption.what_it_hides: The killer actually accompanied Templeton to the yacht and committed the murder upon arrival, not before.

supporting_points: Possession of cigars matching the cigar band found
Lack of alibi for the time of murder
Avoidance of Templeton during his stay
false_solution.the_one_flaw: Grayson was proven to have been elsewhere during the murder and did not have access to the yacht at the critical time.

red_herrings.description: Harold Grayson’s sudden departure and cigar evidence suggested guilt.
red_herrings.innocent_explanation: Grayson left early due to personal reasons unrelated to the murder and was confirmed to be elsewhere during the crime.

red_herrings.description: Isaac Moss’s abrupt departure and nervous behavior raised suspicion.
red_herrings.innocent_explanation: Moss fled out of fear after discovering Templeton’s body and was later corroborated to have an alibi at the hotel.

closed_circle.rationale: All suspects were local or had access to the area and were investigated thoroughly; no outsiders were involved.

inference_path.correction: The stick belonged to the murderer who left it behind

Discovery of identical cigar boxes in Norwood’s house

inference_path.effect: Robbery was not the primary motive

inference_path.correction: Moss fled out of fear, not guilt

inference_path.observation: Grayson left suddenly and had no alibi for murder time
inference_path.correction: Grayson was at Selham and had witnesses

inference_path.observation: Norwood’s walking-stick matched the one found in dinghy
inference_path.correction: Norwood planted a dummy stick and kept original
inference_path.effect: Direct evidence linking Norwood to the crime scene
required_evidence: Colson’s controlled placement of dummy stick in dinghy

discriminating_test.design: Detective Colson secretly replaces the walking-stick in the dinghy with a duplicate. He then watches to see if the suspect attempts to retrieve the stick, confirming possession and guilt. This test uses the walking-stick and the suspect’s behavior as key elements.
discriminating_test.knowledge_revealed: The test reveals that the culprit is aware of the walking-stick’s location and attempts to recover it, confirming his involvement.
discriminating_test.pass_condition: The suspect is observed retrieving the walking-stick from the dinghy during the night.

fair_play_explanation: The reader is given all necessary clues including the walking-stick’s ownership, the cigar band’s change, the diamond transactions, and the suspect’s movements. The detective’s reasoning is laid out clearly, and the false leads are explained and refuted. The incriminating letter and Grice’s confession provide background to motive and identity. Careful attention to the timeline and physical evidence allows the reader to deduce the true culprit.
